claims.text: The proposed framework combines ab initio calculations with machine learning.
The framework explicitly represents oxygen-induced defect configurations and temperature-dependent scattering.
The framework will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr electrical conductivity more accurately than existing perfect-crystal models across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The investigated material includes nearly defect-free HfNbTaTiZr specimens and specimens containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Ionized-impurity scattering is expected to dominate charge transport in the 0–200 K regime.
Phonon or lattice scattering becomes more significant in the 300–1200 K regime.
Oxygen incorporation creates defects that alter local lattice distortions.
Oxygen-induced defects alter local electronic states in HfNbTaTiZr.
The oxygen-induced structural and electronic changes modify charge-carrier scattering rates.
At low temperature, scattering from oxygen-related ionized impurities reduces electron mobility relative to defect-free HfNbTaTiZr.
At high temperature, oxygen-altered lattice structure modifies electron-phonon coupling.
Quantitatively integrating defect scattering and temperature-dependent lattice dynamics will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy.
The proposed model will predict lower conductivity than perfect-crystal analytical models, particularly at low temperature.
The proposed model will capture the complex temperature dependence of conductivity in the 300–1200 K regime.
Existing perfect-crystal analytical approaches tend to overestimate HfNbTaTiZr conductivity because they neglect defect and impurity scattering.
The proposed model is intended for bulk HfNbTaTiZr with nearly defect-free microstructures or approximately 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Model accuracy outside the stated temperature intervals is not established.
A held-out four-probe conductivity benchmark will compare nearly defect-free and 1 wt.% oxygen specimens across both temperature regimes.

The hypothesis is falsified if predictions differ from measurements by more than ±10% across both temperature regimes or if oxygen-containing specimens do not show the predicted conductivity reduction.
